title: The 10 Best Jack Stands
subtitle: 2-ton to 10-ton jack stands with ratchet and double-pin locks for cars, SUVs and trucks, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: Jack stands are what actually hold the car while you're under it; the floor jack only lifts it. We ranked 10 best-selling pairs on rating, review volume and features (a second locking pin, a stated ASME or ANSI safety standard, 3-ton or higher capacity, and a tall reach for trucks). Most stands use a ratchet bar that locks as you raise it; double-locking stands add a pin through the bar as a backup. They run from about $30 a pair to $215 for Sunex's 10-ton pin stands.

avoid.name: Powerbuilt 3 Ton, Bottle Jack and Jack Stands in One, Heavy Duty Vehicle Unijack (620471)
avoid.flag: Capacity stated as both 6,000 and 3,000 lb
avoid.verdict: A jack-and-stand combo whose listing can't agree on how much it holds, sold as one unit for the price of two or three pairs of real stands. Buy a floor jack and a pair of Amazon Basics stands instead.
reasons: The title says 3 tons and 6,000 lb, but the bullets say '3,000-pound capacity.' On something you lie under, the rated load has to be unambiguous.
The title says 'Jack Stands', but you get one unit. Supporting a car properly takes at least two stands, so you'd need two of these at about $200.
It holds the vehicle on a hydraulic bottle jack with a ratchet bar backup. A dedicated mechanical stand doesn't depend on a hydraulic seal at all.

buyers_guide.q: What capacity jack stands do I need?
buyers_guide.a: Ratings are usually per pair. A 3-ton pair covers most cars and small SUVs, since each end of a car carries only part of its weight. Pickups and large SUVs are better on 6-ton stands with a taller range.

Ratchet stands adjust quickly in small steps and lock as you raise them. Pin-type stands lock with a steel pin through the post, which is simple and strong but has fewer heights. Double-locking stands combine both.

buyers_guide.q: Where do I put jack stands?
buyers_guide.a: On the manufacturer's support points (check the owner's manual), usually the pinch welds or frame rails, on hard level ground. Never on suspension arms, the oil pan or asphalt on a hot day.

buyers_guide.q: How do I know the stands are set safely?
buyers_guide.a: Lower the car onto both stands, then push firmly on the car before getting under it. Leave the floor jack lightly raised under a solid point as a backup, and chock the wheels still on the ground.

buyers_guide.q: Do jack stands need a safety standard?
buyers_guide.a: In the U.S., ASME PASE (and the older ANSI/PALD) covers portable automotive lifting and support equipment. A stated standard means the design was tested to it.
